So Linux has a lot of enemies, even as it has a lot of friends, so there's a lot of interest in fucking this up.

systemd and the older systems it replaces ("init systems" of various stripes) do a lot of management for the system overall that the kernel doesn't directly touch. Other OS's have similar designs. The idea is that having one project makes it more vulnerable to corporate takeover, corruption, and the dictates of a crazy person, among many, many others, plus the fact that they're both being shoved down the throat of almost the entire community and they are generally viewed as corrosive to traditional Linux setups and configuration.

Some of the CoC concerns are very similar to this. This could very easily be used by corporations (Microsoft, among others) who have taken a very strong interest in increasing influence in the kernel over the years, e.g. because they'd take over the influence of hobbyists and private developers who want nothing to do with this wretched state of affairs. Additionally corporate interests involved may compromise Linux's core promise and context. For instance, allowing DRM into the kernel and generally, slowly eroding the free software stance through technical compliance but making it practically impossible to take advantage of that compliance, e.g. making it impractical to recompile a new kernel for locked-down hardware, with the distributed kernel having who-knows-what kind of extensions, e.g. perhaps some sort of filter to keep the user out of "bad sites" like Voat. Note also attempts by certain segments of the technology and copyright industry to do things like outlaw the ability to modify your own computing equipment. It would be easy, with proper subversion, to get a situation where the GPL is useless and they can do a lot of terrible things with the kernel, especially if they have corrupt laws on their side, and crap like SOPA and TPP have this as a major part of why they're so terrible.

Now corporate interests interfering in Linux is not the ONLY threat by far, but this is just one example. Unfortunately it's a complex mesh. Some view it as part of a single, overall effort, especially since Red Hat is the one to push systemd the most, and Red Hat's been in bed with other corporate interests for some time with some very questionable political choices (e.g. their involvement with Gnome). It might also be a coincidence. Either way, both of them cause serious issues for traditional Unix/Linux setups which cause a very serious concern for the continued freedom (as in speech, and possibly, eventually, as in beer) involved in the kernel, the technical future of the project, and many other aspects that would probably be able to fill up a book.

Note that Linux, as in the kernel, can and in some distros does exist entirely independently of systemd. See: Slackware, Gentoo, heck, I think Android runs a non-systemd init system. Linux can still run a traditional init system. In fact it could run a shell instead of an init if you really wanted, even if that's of dubious wisdom in non-emergency situations.
